newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's SPD seeks tax deal,but sticks to demands.
newsitem.headline: Germany's SPD seeks tax deal,but sticks to demands.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Sunday affirmed clear differences with the ruling coalition over the shape of possible tax reforms, while asserting readiness to negotiate in key talks this week.

"There must be a breakthrough at the tax negotiations," said SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine, who will meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday to try to avert a parliamentary battle over Kohl's major tax reform project.
But Lafontaine, in a statement, repeated SPD calls for increased child subsidies and a higher minimum for tax-free income than the government has proposed.
Kohl, speaking at the opening of the Hanover Industry Trade Fair, said tax reform remained a key element of his government's strategy to create jobs and a more dynamic economy.
Lower non-wage labour costs, reform of the social security system and investment incentives for the construction industry are further important measures to combat unemployment, Kohl said.
"There are no delaying tactics on my part," he said of Tuesday's planned meeting. "But the plan will not be watered down through poor compromises."

If no agreement is reached in Tuesday's talks, the tax reform bills will have to make their way through a parliamentary mediation committee in the fall. "But I hope we do not have to go that route," Kohl said.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel told the daily Abendzeitung that Lafontaine had abandoned ideas which could have formed the basis of a compromise.
If the SPD was ready to compromise, this would be "a huge success for Germany which the SPD would share in," he said in comments to be published on Monday.
SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said the opposition was ready to bargain, but opposed the government's promise of a net tax reduction of 55 billion marks ($32 billion) a year.
"We are more than open to any proposal the coalition makes," Scharping told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper. A net cut of 10 billion to 15 billion marks was practical, he said.
Scharping also repeated support for an increase in child subsidies, cuts in job insurance contributions and a private asset tax -- ideas coalition leaders criticised at the weekend.
He said an increase in benefit payments to families with children would cost 3.6 billion marks and could be paid for with a new private asset tax.
"The government scrapped this tax and threw between five and six billion marks out the window," he said.
Cuts in employee and employer contributions to job insurance could be paid for later by reducing government bureaucracy and cutting other subsidies, he said.
The SPD wants to cut these job overheads by July 1 to help to ease Germany's near-record unemployment, which fell by 190,000 in March to 4.3 million.

But the July 1 date will be out of reach unless the government agrees to the cuts on Tuesday, said Lafontaine, who called for the child subsidy rise and job overhead reductions on Friday in a list of demands for the tax talks.

Kohl's closest aide, Wolfgang Schaeuble, told the news weekly Der Spiegel the coalition was ready to discuss "all points, all proposals," but had doubts "whether the SPD is serious and wants to cooperate on reform."
Kohl's coalition has sought cuts of 30 billion marks in income and corporate taxes over two years to try to revive the economy to meet criteria for European monetary union.

The SPD quit the tax talks in February in a row over coal subsidies. If the latest talks fail, the reform battle will move to parliament, where the SPD can block tax measures through its majority in the upper house.
